subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discourse marker such as 'however' or 'furthermore'?
options: To signal the relationship between ideas and guide the reader
questions.explain: Discourse markers connect ideas and show contrast, addition or sequence to aid coherence.

questions.q: You are writing a leaflet for a local charity event. Which feature is most appropriate to the form?
options: Clear headings, bullet points and key details like time and place
A single dense block of text
questions.explain: Leaflets use headings, bullets and signposting so readers can scan key information quickly.

questions.q: "Do we really want our children breathing this filthy air?" Which technique is this?
questions.explain: It is a question asked for effect, not for an answer: a rhetorical question.

questions.q: Which sentence best uses 'show, not tell' to convey that a character is nervous?
options: She was very nervous about the exam.
Her hands trembled as she gripped the pencil, her eyes fixed on the clock.
The girl was nervous because of the test.
She felt nervous and scared inside.
questions.explain: Showing physical detail lets the reader infer the emotion rather than stating it outright.

questions.q: Which technique is being used: 'Imagine a world where no child goes to bed hungry'?
options: Direct address and an emotive appeal
questions.explain: It speaks directly to the reader ('Imagine') and triggers an emotional response.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the most ambitious, precise vocabulary?
options: The big house was really old and bad.
The house was very very scary.
The derelict mansion loomed, its decaying facade menacing the street.
The old house was scary and big.
questions.explain: 'Derelict', 'loomed', 'decaying' and 'menacing' are precise, ambitious word choices.

questions.q: Which is the most effective, vivid sensory description of a market?
options: Spices stung the air, voices clashed overhead, and ripe mangoes glistened on every stall.
The market was busy and had lots of things.
The market was a place where you could buy stuff.
There were many people at the market buying food.
questions.explain: It engages multiple senses (smell, sound, sight) to create an immersive image.

questions.q: You are writing a speech. Which feature would make it most engaging for a live audience?
options: A repeated phrase used as a rallying refrain
Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense detail
questions.explain: Repetition (anaphora) builds rhythm and impact, ideal for spoken delivery.

questions.q: A travel article says "You will love every breathtaking moment of this paradise." What is its main PURPOSE?
options: To persuade the reader to visit
questions.explain: Positive, emotive language directed at "you" is designed to persuade the reader to go.

questions.q: "It was cruel, heartless and utterly inhumane." The use of three linked words for emphasis is called:
questions.explain: Three items grouped for rhetorical force is tripling (a triplet/rule of three).

questions.q: What does 'planning' your writing before you start mainly help you to do?
options: Organise ideas logically and avoid drifting off task
questions.explain: Planning structures ideas in advance so the writing stays coherent and on-task.

questions.q: Which is an effective way to vary sentence length for tension in narrative writing?
options: Follow several longer sentences with a short, punchy one: 'He stopped.'
questions.explain: A sudden short sentence after longer ones creates emphasis and tension.
